cases.note: Divergence: GNU bash 5.2.37 prints "a\nrest", because head -c reads only the bytes it needs from a pipe. Mirage's readers take a pipe chunk by chunk, so the first reader takes the rest of the chunk the producer wrote with it.

cases.command: f() { local a b; read -r a < "$1"; read -r b < "$1"; echo "[$a][$b]"; }; f <(printf '1\n2\n')
cases.note: Divergence: GNU bash 5.2.37 prints "[1][2]\n", because read takes a pipe a byte at a time. Mirage's line reader takes the chunk the producer wrote, and the rest of it goes with the first read's redirect.

head -c 1 <(head -c 100000 /dev/zero; echo after >&2) | od -An -c
cases.note: Divergence: GNU bash 5.2.37 also prints "after\n" on stderr: SIGPIPE ends only the substitution's writer and its next command runs. In Mirage the substitution's line ends when its reader closes early.

cases.note: Mirage refuses exec onto a process substitution, which lives only as long as the command naming it (GNU bash 5.2.37 prints "hi\nend\n"); the later write to the unopened descriptor fails as any write to one does.

cases.command: (set -o pipefail; cat <(head -c 200000 /dev/zero) | head -c 1 | od -An -c; echo "st=$? ${PIPESTATUS[*]}")
cases.note: Divergence: GNU bash 5.2.37 prints "  \\0\nst=141 141 0 0\n": the substitution's writer dies of SIGPIPE and cat reports it. In Mirage the substitution's line ends quietly when its reader closes early, so pipefail sees no failure.
